## This week in the cycle

<div class="steps"><div><b>Question</b></div><div><b>Data</b></div><div class="hot"><b>Cleaning</b></div><div class="hot"><b>Exploration</b></div><div><b>Analysis</b></div><div><b>Conclusions</b></div><div><b>Reproduce</b></div></div>

- **Read** a real file correctly, and check it.
- **Shape** it with five verbs.
- **Summarise** groups: size, centre, spread, and uncertainty when the data are a sample.

## Reading a real file

```text
LÄNSKOD;KOMMUNKOD;LÄNSNAMN;KOMMUNNAMN;M;C;…;VALDELTAGANDE
1;14;Stockholms län;Upplands Väsby;23,11;6,26;…;84,7
```

| You see | It means | Tell the function |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `;` | semicolon separator | `sep=";"` · `read_csv2()` |
| `23,11` | decimal comma | `decimal=","` · `read_csv2()` |
| `Ä`, `Ö` | encoding matters | `encoding="utf-8-sig"` |

<div class="keyline">Defaults fail loudly, or worse, silently: with only <code>sep=";"</code>, turnout is read as <b>text</b>.</div>

## Check what you got

```python
raw.shape     # (290, 45): the number of rows you expected?
raw.dtypes    # numbers as numbers, not text?
raw.head()    # does it look like the file?
```

- Three lines, right after reading, every time.
- Recompute a column from its parts: `voters / electorate` should match the turnout column.
- **Never** open the raw file in Excel and save it.

## Tidy data

:::: cols
::: {}
**Tidy:** one row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell.

| municipality | county | turnout |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Haparanda | Norrbotten | 72.8 |
| Lomma | Skåne | 93.9 |
:::
::: {}
**Not tidy:** a variable hidden in the column names.

| municipality | 2014 | 2018 |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Haparanda | … | 72.8 |
| Lomma | … | 93.9 |
:::
::::

<p class="small muted">Tools expect tidy tables. Reshaping between the two is week 3.</p>

## The five verbs

| Verb | pandas | dplyr |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **select** columns | `df[["a", "b"]]` | `select(a, b)` |
| **filter** rows | `df.query("a > 1")` | `filter(a > 1)` |
| **mutate**: a new column | `df.assign(c=...)` | `mutate(c = ...)` |
| **arrange**: sort | `df.sort_values("a")` | `arrange(a)` |
| **group and summarise** | `df.groupby("g").agg(...)` | `group_by(g) \|> summarise(...)` |

<p class="small muted">Almost everything you do to a table combines these five. One step per line, so a reviewer can comment on each.</p>

## Summarise every group the same way

| County | n | mean | median | sd |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Norrbotten | 14 | 84.3 | 85.3 | 4.3 |
| Västerbotten | 15 | 85.2 | 85.0 | 2.1 |
| … | | | | |
| Gotland | 1 | 88.8 | 88.8 | – |
| Östergötland | 13 | 88.9 | 89.1 | 1.1 |

- **n:** Gotland is one municipality. No spread, an unreliable "mean".
- **mean vs median:** Haparanda drags Norrbotten's mean down.
- **spread vs difference:** within some counties, municipalities differ by more than counties do.

## Sample or population?

:::: cols
::: {}
**The election: all 290 municipalities.**

The table *is* the 2018 result. There is no sampling uncertainty to report.
:::
::: {}
**HW2: 158 apartment sales.**

Some of the sales that could have happened. Each group mean gets its interval:

$$\bar x \pm 1.96\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$$
:::
::::

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../statistics#_4-how-sure-are-you-standard-errors-and-confidence-intervals">Statistics, section 4</a></p>

## Start the axis at zero, for bars

<img src="../../img/week-2/misleading-axis.svg" alt="The same three means drawn with the axis from 84% and from 0%">

<p>Left: Östergötland's bar looks fifteen times as long. Its turnout is 4.5 points higher, about 5% more.</p>

<div class="keyline">The eye reads a bar's <b>length</b>. To show small differences, use dots.</div>

## A log scale for sizes

<img src="../../img/week-2/turnout-size.svg" alt="Turnout against electorate on a log scale; no strong pattern">

<p class="small">From 1 886 to 704 157 people entitled to vote: each step on the axis is ten times the last. Say so on the axis. No strong pattern: size alone says little about turnout.</p>

## Honest plots: a checklist

::: twocol
1. The caption says what to see.
2. Axes labelled, with units.
3. Bars start at zero.
4. Show the data, not only summaries.
5. Show uncertainty when it is a sample.
6. Same scale on panels you compare.
7. No 3D, no second y-axis.
8. State any transformation.
:::

## A review that helps

| Less helpful | More helpful |
|:--|:--|
| "The plot is confusing." | "The y-axis starts at 50 000, so the 1-room bar looks twice the 3-room bar. Start at zero, or use dots." |
| "Good job!" | "The table with n and an interval per group made the conclusion easy to check." |
| "Wrong numbers." | "Line 42 drops every row with any missing value, so all 158 sales are gone. Drop only rows missing `livingArea`." |

<p class="small muted">Comment on a line in <b>Files changed</b>; use suggestion blocks for small fixes.</p>

## HW2: Tables and plots

**How does the price per m² depend on the number of rooms, in Ekhagen?**

- 158 apartment sales, 2012–2018.
- Your choices: how to group the rooms, what to drop. Write down why.
- A group table with **n, mean, median, sd and a 95% interval**.
- A figure that shows **every sale**, and the means with their intervals.
- Prices rose over 2012–2018. Could that affect your answer?
